title: Builder versus Factory Method, and what a Director does

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: How does the Builder pattern differ from the Factory pattern?

options.text: A Builder picks the concrete class, and a Factory fills in the optional fields.
options.says: It is the other way round: choosing which type to create is the factory's concern, and optional parameters are the builder's.

options.text: A Builder assembles an object over several calls, and a Factory creates it in one.
options.says: The page contrasts step-by-step construction by a builder with one-step creation by a factory.

options.text: A Builder cannot run without a Director, and a Factory needs no helper at all.
options.says: The Director is optional: the fluent builder common in Java has none, and the client drives the steps itself.

questions.stem: In the GoF form of the Builder pattern, what is the Director responsible for?

options.text: Returning this from each builder method so that calls can be chained.
options.says: Returning this is the mark of the fluent (Effective Java) builder, which has no Director at all.

options.text: Holding the product's constructor so that no client can call it directly.
options.says: Keeping the constructor private is the product's own job; the Director only drives the builder.

options.text: Calling the building steps in a set order on whichever builder it is given.
options.says: The Director orchestrates the steps, so one construction process can yield different representations from different builders.

origin.section: Two Styles of Builder in Java

concepts: A Builder assembles one complex object step by step under the client's control, where a Factory Method creates an object in one step and a subclass picks its type.
The Director belongs to the GoF Builder and defines the order of construction steps; the fluent builder has none and returns this for chaining.
